narrative:
The model estimated an 82.3% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, so your law school application was rejected. This is a prediction, not a final judgment, but it means the application as submitted raised serious concern about first-time bar success.

The strongest reason was your third-year academic standing. You were in the second decile of your class, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this was the largest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your first-year standing was the second most influential factor and also pushed toward failure: you were again in the second decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, and it worked in your favor: at 2.90 it is below the accepted-student average of about 3.23, but it still nudged the model toward passing rather than failing. It was not strong enough to offset the concerns about your law-school academic standing.

To improve your chances, focus on evidence that addresses those concerns: consider retaking the LSAT, taking additional coursework or a structured bar-preparation program, and obtaining academic advising. You may also strengthen your application with work or legal experience and apply to a balanced range of schools. Ask admissions offices what specific improvements would make a future application more competitive.
